rationale: A wins by a slight margin because it keeps the investor story cleanly separated from the margin-disclosure story: "A still-unprofitable public chain is betting the path to profit runs through automation" is a real equities angle, not a press-release costume. B is serious work, but "Sweetgreen moves the automated kitchen from pilot to standard spec for new stores" smuggles in a pilot-to-standard narrative the update never gave it. When the facts are thin, the set that resists decorating them gets the nod.
gaps_in_A: "robot-assembled stores" and "human-run ones" punch up the facts. The update gives an automated conveyor system with minimal staff versus traditional stores, not necessarily robots versus humans.
"Is there any current news peg here? None was supplied." The company expansion and margin disclosure are the current peg; the cleaner critique is that no outside newsjack peg was supplied.
"restaurant-sector analyst-desk" is a little mushy as journalist shape. Analysts are useful sources or readers, but the target should stay with markets/equities reporters.
gaps_in_B: "automated stores earn more" blurs margin with earnings. The update supports higher restaurant-level margins and faster throughput, not higher revenue or profit.
"from pilot to standard spec" and "single flagship test" invent a rollout history. The facts say expansion, most new stores, and some retrofits; they do not say pilot, flagship, or standard spec.
"telling investors" is an inference, not a supplied fact. Sweetgreen is public and shared margin data, but the audience and venue of the disclosure are not given.
"where fast-casual build specs are heading" ladders one chain into a category trend without competitor or industry evidence. Useful angle, but it needs more proof before it can carry that altitude.
